title: What's this? — things, articles, and numbers
goal: Name the things around you, use the article -a and the plural -ak, point with hau/hori/hura, and count to twenty.
bekal: stick *-a* and *-ak* onto the end of a noun — a "the" that goes at the back
tell *hau*, *hori*, *hura* apart — three pointing distances, like "this, that, that over there"
count from zero to twenty and ask *zenbat?*

dialogs.title: Elkarrizketa — Gela berria
dialogs.intro: Ainhoa shows Budi his room in an apartment near the euskaltegi.

lines.speaker: Ainhoa:
lines.text: Hau zure gela da. Handia da, ezta?
lines.id: This is your room. It's big, isn't it?
lines.literal: this your room-the is. big-the is, not-so?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bai, oso handia. Eta hori zer da?
lines.id: Yes, very big. And what's that?

lines.speaker: Ainhoa:
lines.text: Hori mahaia da. Eta hau aulkia.
lines.id: That's the table. And this is the chair.
lines.literal: that table-the is. and this chair-the.

lines.text: Ez, bi aulki daude. Bestea han dago.
lines.id: No, there are two chairs. The other one is over there.
lines.literal: no, two chair are(located). other-the there is(located).

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ados. Eta liburu horiek zer dira?
lines.id: OK. And what are those books?
lines.literal: agreed. and book those what are?

lines.speaker: Ainhoa:
lines.id: They're books in Basque. For you.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you! How many books are there?

lines.speaker: Ainhoa:
lines.text: Bai, berri-berria. Gela polita da, ezta?
lines.id: Yes, brand-new. It's a nice room, isn't it?
lines.literal: yes, new-new-the. room-the pretty-the is, not-so?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bai, oso polita. Hemen gustura nago.
lines.id: Yes, very nice. I feel at home here.

notes: **Ezta? means "isn't it?" / "right?".** Tacked onto the end of a sentence to ask for agreement. It comes from *ez da* ("it isn't"), but it's now one word and never changes — unlike English tags (isn't it, don't you, aren't they), it works for any sentence.

**Numbers go first — except one.** *Hamar liburu* (ten books), *bi aulki* (two chairs) — the number comes first. But *bat* ("one") goes after: *aulki bat*, *hiztegi bat*. That's because *bat* also works as "a/an", and markers of indefiniteness always come last in this language.
**Counted nouns don't take the plural.** *Hamar liburu*, not *hamar liburuak* — literally "ten book". Unlike English, once the number is there, the noun stays bare.

**Berri-berria — doubling for emphasis.** Basque doubles an adjective to mean "very": *berri-berria* (brand-new), *bete-betea* (full to the brim), *goxo-goxoa* (really delicious). Think of English "a big, big house" — except in Basque it's a fixed pattern.

blocks.text: This is the first rule you really need to master, and the good news is that it's completely regular. Nouns in the dictionary stand bare — *etxe*, *liburu*, *mahai*. As soon as one is used in a sentence as a specific thing, it gets *-a* on its tail.

The *neska* row shows the one exception you need to remember: a word that **already** ends in *-a* doesn't add another *-a*. *Neska* means both "girl" and "the girl"; the plural is just *neskak*. There are lots of words like this — *ama* (mother), *alaba* (daughter), *hizkuntza* (language).
Adjectives go after the noun, and the article moves there too
If there's an adjective, it comes **after** the noun — and *-a* moves to the end of the whole group, sticking to the adjective.

blocks.title: The most common mistakes
items: Putting *-a* in two places: ***etxea handia*** is wrong. The right form is *etxe handia* — one group, one article, at the very end.
Using the bare dictionary word as a subject: ***Etxe handia da*** sounds like a half-finished sentence. The right form is *Etxea handia da* (the house is big).
A quick test: if English would say "the", Basque needs *-a* (or *-ak*) at the end of the group.

blocks.text: Basque has three pointing distances, not two: *this* (near me), *that* (near you), and *that over there* (far from both of us) — like the old English "yonder".

On its own, it's the subject of the sentence: *Hau mahaia da* (this is a table). Used with a noun, it stands **after** it, and the noun then drops the *-a*: *liburu hau* (this book), *liburu horiek* (those books), *gela hura* (that room over there).

blocks.title: Hura has two jobs
items: *Hura* means "that (over there)" and also **"he/she"** for people. *Hura irakaslea da* can mean "he/she is a teacher" or "that one over there is the teacher" — context decides.
Basque has no separate words for "he" and "she". One less thing to memorize.

blocks.text: From 11 to 17 the pattern is clear: *hama-* (from *hamar*, ten) plus the number — *hamabi* = ten-two. Eighteen and nineteen break the pattern as *hemezortzi* and *hemeretzi*; just learn them as they are.
Ask "how many" with *zenbat*, and leave the noun bare: *Zenbat liburu?* (how many books?), *Zenbat urte?* (how many years?). The answer has no article either: *Hamar liburu.*

blocks.title: A small warning about bigger numbers
items: Basque counts in **twenties**, not tens. Forty is *berrogei* — literally "two times twenty". Sixty is *hirurogei*, "three times twenty".
If you've met French, it's the same habit as *quatre-vingts* (eighty = four twenties) — or English "four score". The difference is that Basque uses it for all the tens.
Numbers 21 to 100 are covered fully in Unit 3. For now, twenty is enough for almost any first conversation.
That house over there is big.
